newsitem.title: USA: USDA to whittle away 1,320 more jobs.
newsitem.headline: USDA to whittle away 1,320 more jobs.

text.p: The U.S. Agriculture Department aims to cut about 1,320 administrative jobs over the next five years, mostly in the rural offices that help farmers with government programmes, the agency said on Friday.
The planned job cuts would save an estimated $449 million, according to a memo written by Agriculture Secretary Dan Glickman. The memo was made public on Friday.

The brunt of the cuts would come in the Farm Service Agency, which helps farmers qualify for and comply with programs; the Natural Resources Conservation Service, which provides technical assistance to farmers; and rural development agencies that provide housing, business and utilities service.

"Unless we simplify our administrative overhead and reduce costs, we will not have credibility when we ask the Congress to appropriate funds for our programmes and we will ultimately be unable to provide adequate services to our customers," Glickman said in the memo to key deputies.

Glickman's decision to cut overhead positions comes in the midst of a broader downsizing at the Agriculture Department, where about 11,000 workers already were scheduled to lose their jobs over the next four years.
Some agriculture groups have expressed concern that government services that farmers are accustomed to getting may be reduced.

The number of Agriculture Department employees assigned to county offices has been reduced by nearly 14 percent since 1993, and plans are in place to pare staffing further for a total cut of 40 percent in 2002 compared with 1993.
News of the further downsizing drew applause from Sen. Richard Lugar, chairman of the Senate Agriculture committee which oversees the agency.
"At the county, state and national level, USDA's mission has changed significantly and so too should its structure," Lugar said.
At Lugar's prodding, the Agriculture Department already has consolidated 43 divisions into 28, closed 1,200 field offices and made other budget cuts expected to save $2.3 billion over five years.

Under the new proposed cuts, each state will have one administrative staff group, except for states with small geographic areas and light workloads that can share administrative staffs, the memo said.
The proposed job cuts are designed to shift money into computer modernisation and to protect basic services.
Between 500 and 600 administrative jobs would be lost at the department's Washington headquarters, according to the proposal.
